figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: StartLux-Decision leads at every evaluated scale on the public subset of Decision Index 0.3.
figures.headline: Instant models lead at every evaluated scale on the public Decision Index 0.3 subset, with the 4B Instant model above all reference models.
citing_sentences: On the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, the Instant models outperform the strongest evaluated comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4–16.9 points, with the 4B Instant model surpassing all evaluated reference decision models (Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Training and inference workflows of StartLux-Decision. (a) Three-stage training establishes shared decision capabilities, specializes the Instant and AutoThink variants, and develops explicit reasoning in AutoThink through reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning. Instant adopts bidirectional attention in full-attention layers, while AutoThink retains causal attention. (b) Instant produces decision probabilities in a single forward pass, whereas AutoThink first obtains an initial prediction $p_{0}$ and selectively invokes reasoning based on its confidence. When reasoning is invoked, the post-reasoning prediction $p_{1}$ is combined with $p_{0}$ to form the final decision.
figures.headline: Training has three stages, and inference either makes one pass for Instant or reads confidence to decide whether AutoThink reasons.
citing_sentences: A three-stage training pipeline establishes shared decision capabilities, specializes the two variants, and equips AutoThink with explicit reasoning through reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning (Figure 2; Section 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: AutoThink selectively invokes reasoning for uncertain decisions. Top: Two cases from the same DecisionPivot policy illustrate confidence-guided inference, with direct prediction for a confident case and reasoning-assisted correction for an uncertain case. Bars show decision probabilities, with correct options highlighted in green. Bottom: Across 7,800 core DecisionPivot items, the 27B AutoThink model makes direct predictions on 39% of cases with 96% accuracy and invokes reasoning for the remaining 61%. On reasoning-invoked cases, accuracy improves from 57% before reasoning to 93% after default-answer fusion, with 1,783 initial errors corrected and 94 new errors introduced.
figures.headline: On DecisionPivot, reasoning lifts the 27B AutoThink model's uncertain cases from 57% to 93% accuracy, correcting 1,783 initial errors.
citing_sentences: Figure 3 illustrates Read-or-Think using two cases from the same data-export policy in DecisionPivot.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Bidirectional attention improves single-pass decision performance across most evaluated model scales. (a) Causal and bidirectional attention patterns in full-attention layers, with linear-attention layers remaining causal and decision probabilities read from the final prompt position. (b) DI 0.3 performance of Stage 2 models trained on identical data from the same Stage 1 checkpoint, differing only in their attention configurations. Runs with identical training configurations exhibit variations of 0.2–0.7 index points across random seeds.
figures.headline: Bidirectional attention improves Decision Index 0.3 performance at four of five scales, by up to 2.4 points.
citing_sentences: At 4B and 9B, this modification applies to 8 of the 32 layers, while the linear-attention layers and option-letter readout remain unchanged (Figure 4a).

Controlled comparisons using identical training data and the same Stage 1 checkpoint show that bidirectional attention improves DI 0.3 performance at four of the five evaluated model scales, with gains of up to 2.4 points (Figure 4b).
In a controlled Stage 2 comparison using identical data and the same Stage 1 checkpoint (Figure 4b), causal and bidirectional models score 50.3 and 64.9 on MuSR, respectively.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: RLCD2 improves termination and efficiency while largely preserving held-out accuracy. The 4B, 9B, and 27B AutoThink models before RL (gray) and after RLCD2 (violet), using the decision-weighted score and a soft penalty budget of 3,072 tokens (distinct from the 4,096-token generation limit). Held-out metrics are measured on 2,986 examples with reasoning invoked for every example: default-answer accuracy, termination rate, mean trace length, and post-reasoning calibration error before temperature scaling. DecisionPivot pair accuracy is measured on 7,800 core items at the default confidence gate of 0.9.
figures.headline: After RLCD2, 9B reasoning termination rises from 45.9% to 93.9% while held-out accuracy stays largely unchanged.
citing_sentences: The primary benefits of RLCD2 are improved reasoning termination and reduced generation cost (Table 2; Figure 5).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: RLCD2 improves decisions with previously unterminated traces but can reduce accuracy on long computations. Change in DecisionPivot accuracy at the default gate, after RL minus before RL, grouped by pre-RL trace length. Error bars show 95% intervals, and $n$ denotes the number of items in each group.
figures.headline: RLCD2 improves DecisionPivot items with previously unterminated traces but can reduce accuracy on long computations.
citing_sentences: To identify where these trade-offs arise, we group DecisionPivot examples by their pre-RL reasoning lengths (Figure 6).

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: The Instant models outperform comparable-scale reference decision models by 7.4–16.9 points on the public subset of DI 0.3. Scores are plotted against parameter count. The gray line connects the strongest evaluated third-party model at each scale, all from the Decision 3.0 family of vLLM Semantic Router. Jev is hosted, with an undisclosed parameter count.
figures.headline: Plotted against parameter count, the Instant models sit above the strongest comparable-scale reference model at each scale.
citing_sentences: Across all five parameter scales, the Instant models outperform the strongest evaluated comparable-scale third-party decision models, all from the Decision 3.0 family, by 7.4–16.9 points on the public subset of DI 0.3 (Figure 7).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: The 27B Instant model outperforms all evaluated reference decision models across the five DI 0.3 domains. Overall and domain scores are reported in points on the public subset, with domain weights matching the leaderboard. Solid bars show Instant performance, while hatched extensions represent the score differences between AutoThink and Instant at each scale. When AutoThink scores lower, the dashed line marks the higher Instant score. Reference scores come from the public leaderboard, except for Decision 3.0 d3, which we evaluate using the same pipeline as StartLux-Decision.
figures.headline: The 27B Instant model outperforms all evaluated reference decision models across the five Decision Index 0.3 domains.
citing_sentences: In this domain, the 4B and 9B AutoThink models outperform their Instant counterparts by 7.0 and 6.2 points, respectively (Figure 8).

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: The 27B AutoThink model achieves the highest pair accuracy among evaluated systems on DecisionPivot. Results cover 7,800 examples across 13 programmatically generated task families, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Solid bars show single-pass performance, while hatched extensions indicate the gains of AutoThink over Instant at the default confidence threshold of 0.9.
figures.headline: The 27B AutoThink model reaches 86.9% pair accuracy on DecisionPivot, the highest among evaluated systems.
citing_sentences: The 27B Instant model achieves 75.4% pair accuracy, outperforming Decision 3.0 d3 (71.3%), Perplexity Decider v1.1 (70.1%), and the hosted Jev (31.0%), while GLM-5.3 reaches 82.2% with explicit reasoning (Figure 9).

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: AutoThink excels on computation-intensive decisions, while strong single-pass models remain competitive on structural tasks. Pair accuracy is reported in percent across the 13 DecisionPivot core families, with darker cells indicating higher scores. StartLux-Decision models are shown in violet and reference systems in gray.
figures.headline: AutoThink gains most on computation-intensive families, while single-pass models stay competitive on structural tasks.
citing_sentences: The family-level results reveal distinct strengths across computational and structural decision tasks (Figure 10).

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: StartLux-Decision achieves lower calibration error than evaluated reference decision models on DecisionPivot. Left: empirical accuracy versus predicted confidence (maximum option probability) for the 4B, 9B, and 27B AutoThink models and hosted Jev across 7,800 core examples. Points below the diagonal indicate overconfidence. Right: calibration error based on confidence–accuracy gaps across 15 bins, reported in percentage points. Bars show AutoThink at the default confidence threshold of 0.9, with dashed lines marking the corresponding Instant models.
figures.headline: StartLux-Decision models show lower calibration error than the reference decision models on DecisionPivot.
citing_sentences: On 7,800 DecisionPivot core examples, we compare predicted confidence, defined as the maximum option probability, with empirical accuracy across 15 confidence bins (Figure 11).
The evaluated StartLux-Decision models exhibit lower calibration error than the reference systems shown in Figure 11.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: AutoThink outperforms Instant on computation-intensive tasks across all three evaluated scales. Solid bars show Instant accuracy, while hatched extensions indicate accuracy differences between the complete model variants. AutoThink uses the default confidence threshold of 0.9. Results cover the 4B, 9B, and 27B models on 2,638 reconstructed GSM8K problems from DI 0.3, along with CRUXEval, GPQA Diamond, and MMLU-Pro from DI 0.2.1 (Table D.1).
figures.headline: AutoThink outperforms Instant on computation-intensive tasks at all three scales, including reconstructed GSM8K problems.
citing_sentences: AutoThink exhibits its largest advantages over Instant on tasks requiring multi-step computation (Figure 12).

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Confidence-guided reasoning captures most of the attainable accuracy gains, while RLCD2 reduces reasoning cost at 4B and 9B. Accuracy is plotted against average reasoning tokens per example, including those answered without reasoning, as the confidence threshold varies from 0 (never reason) to 1 (always reason). Stars indicate the default threshold of 0.9. The top row evaluates 2,986 held-out examples from the training distribution; the bottom row reports pair accuracy on 7,800 DecisionPivot core examples. Each model scale uses its own token axis. Solid curves represent the released AutoThink models after RLCD2, while dashed gray curves represent their pre-RLCD2 checkpoints.
figures.headline: Routing low-confidence predictions to reasoning captures most accuracy gains, and RLCD2 reduces reasoning cost at 4B and 9B.
citing_sentences: Within each AutoThink checkpoint, varying the confidence threshold from 0 (never reason) to 1 (always reason) reveals the accuracy–computation trade-off (Figure 13).

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Decision probabilities respond to supporting evidence and become more consistent across related question formulations as model scale increases. Results use single-pass readouts of the released models. (a) Mean change in the supported answer’s probability after removing a supporting sentence from HoVer or a gold paragraph from HotpotQA. Control perturbations add an irrelevant sentence or remove a distractor paragraph, producing mean changes within 0.015 of zero. (b) Mean absolute deviation of the summed affirmative probabilities from one when each candidate option is independently reformulated as a yes-or-no question, reported for binary questions and for the full set of questions.
figures.headline: Predicted probabilities fall when supporting evidence is removed, and consistency across reformulations improves with model scale.
citing_sentences: By contrast, adding an irrelevant sentence or removing a distractor paragraph changes the corresponding probability by less than 0.015 on average (Figure 14a).

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Selection and routing induce miscalibration that policy-aware calibration mitigates without retraining the underlying models. (a) Accuracy of responses selected by a 9B verifier from $N$ candidates, restricted to reported confidence of 80–90%. Shaded bands indicate variation across 20 splits. (b) Mean absolute confidence–accuracy gaps across 184 settings spanning best-of-$N$, think-gate, cascade, and select-then-think pipelines. Policy-aware calibration reduces these gaps across all four pipelines, with signed gaps ranging from $-2.7$ to $+2.1$ percentage points.
figures.headline: Selected responses become less accurate as the candidate pool grows, and policy-aware calibration reduces gaps across all four pipelines.
citing_sentences: Calibrating individual responses does not eliminate this effect: selected-response accuracy at fixed confidence declines as the candidate pool grows (Figure 15a).

Across 184 settings spanning best-of-$N$, think-gate, cascade, and select-then-think pipelines, policy-aware calibration reduces signed confidence–accuracy gaps from $[-11.7,+20.5]$ to $[-2.7,+2.1]$ percentage points (Figure 15b).

abstract: We introduce StartLux-Decision, state-of-the-art decision models spanning 0.8B–27B parameters, combining efficient single-pass prediction with adaptive, confidence-guided reasoning. The Instant models leverage bidirectional attention in full-attention layers to improve decision accuracy while preserving efficient single-pass inference. The AutoThink models selectively invoke explicit reasoning for uncertain decisions while answering confident cases directly. We develop a three-stage training pipeline that establishes shared decision capabilities, specializes the two variants, and equips AutoThink with explicit reasoning through reasoning supervision and reinforcement learning. To improve reasoning efficiency while preserving decision quality, we introduce Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions (RLCD2). Extending decision-oriented reinforcement learning to explicit reasoning, RLCD2 uses a frozen model and proper scoring rules to reward improvements in decision probability quality, while imposing a soft penalty on overlong reasoning traces. RLCD2 increases the proportion of reasoning traces that terminate within the generation limit by up to 48 percentage points and reduces average reasoning length by up to 65%, while largely preserving decision accuracy. On the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, the Instant models outperform the strongest evaluated comparable-scale open-weight decision models by 7.4–16.9 points, with the 27B AutoThink model further improving its score to 73.4. We also introduce DecisionPivot, a programmatically verifiable benchmark of computational decisions featuring contrast pairs that differ in a single answer-changing detail. On DecisionPivot, AutoThink consistently outperforms its Instant counterparts by 11.5–18.4 percentage points in pair accuracy and achieves leading performance among evaluated systems, highlighting the benefits of adaptive reasoning for computation-intensive decisions. To facilitate practical deployment, we support inference across vLLM, llama.cpp, and MLX, together with quantized model variants for reduced memory requirements. We envision StartLux-Decision advancing a new generation of decision models that adaptively allocate reasoning to challenging decisions, balancing decision quality, computational efficiency, and reliability.

sections.body: The introduction defines a decision model as one that answers typed questions with probability distributions over candidate options, which downstream systems use to act, escalate, or defer. It states that single-pass open-weight decision models can struggle with computation-intensive decisions, and that decision-oriented training can impair reasoning generation and termination. The paper presents two variants sharing one probability interface: Instant, which uses bidirectional attention in full-attention layers, and AutoThink, which reasons only on uncertain decisions. It introduces RLCD2, reporting termination up to 48 percentage points higher and reasoning length reduced by up to 65%. It also introduces DecisionPivot, where AutoThink beats Instant by 11.5–18.4 percentage points in pair accuracy, and policy-aware calibration, which reduces gaps to within 2.7 percentage points across 184 settings.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Decision models need reasoning on hard cases without losing single-pass efficiency; the paper proposes two variants, RLCD2 training, and DecisionPivot.

sections.body: Instant models use bidirectional attention in the full-attention layers, applied to 8 of 32 layers at 4B and 9B, and are trained that way rather than only at inference. AutoThink uses Read-or-Think: it makes a one-pass prediction, then reasons with a trace of up to 4,096 tokens when the maximum probability is below 0.9. It blends the initial and post-reasoning distributions with a weight of 0.75 on the post-reasoning distribution. All models share an option-letter readout trained with soft cross-entropy and calibrated with per-question-type temperatures. Controlled comparisons show bidirectional attention improves Decision Index 0.3 at four of five scales, with gains of up to 2.4 points. On reasoning-invoked cases in DecisionPivot, the 27B model's accuracy rises from 57% to 93%.
sections.heading: Model Design and Training
sections.headline: Three-stage training gives Instant bidirectional attention and teaches AutoThink to reason only when its confidence is below 0.9.

sections.body: RLCD2 keeps a frozen copy of the starting model to give probability readouts before and after a reasoning trace. The reward is the decision-weighted proper score after reasoning minus the score before, minus $10^{-4}$ per token beyond a soft budget. Traces ending within eight tokens get zero reward, and training uses only questions whose initial maximum probability is below 0.9. On held-out examples at 9B, termination rises from 45.9% to 93.9% and mean trace length falls from 2,494 to 868 tokens, a 65% reduction. At 4B, termination rises from 89.5% to 99.3%, and held-out accuracy changes fall within uncertainty intervals that include zero. The authors report that long computations can still lose accuracy, with a 4.2-point loss at 4B for pre-RL traces of 2,048–4,095 tokens under the 3,072-token budget.
sections.heading: RLCD2: Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Deliberative Decisions
sections.headline: RLCD2 rewards reasoning by the change in proper score and penalizes traces beyond a soft budget.

sections.body: The evaluation uses Decision Index 0.2.1, with 38 benchmarks, and the public subset of Decision Index 0.3, which accounts for 20% of the leaderboard score. The public subset also served as the development benchmark, so its scores reflect model selection. DecisionPivot has 13 core families of 600 examples each, 7,800 items in total, scored by pair accuracy, which requires both items in a pair to be correct. The 27B Instant model reaches 75.4% pair accuracy against 71.3% for Decision 3.0 d3, and the 27B AutoThink model reaches 86.9%. AutoThink exceeds Instant by 18.4, 12.4, and 11.5 points at 4B, 9B, and 27B. Calibration error for AutoThink is 2.4, 3.3, and 5.2 points at those scales, against 7.3, 6.4, and 5.1 for Instant. The 27B AutoThink model is the only StartLux-Decision model that is underconfident on average.
sections.heading: Experimental Evaluation
sections.headline: On the public Decision Index 0.3 subset, Instant models lead comparable-scale references by 7.4–16.9 points.

sections.body: This section examines what drives gains and whether confidence stays reliable downstream. Adding Stage 2 data improves the 18 matched DecisionPivot tasks by 8.6 points, versus 0.3 points for tasks outside those families, which indicates task-family specialization. Bidirectional attention improves 16 tasks whose families are absent from a narrower mixture by 3.0 points. For adaptive reasoning, the 27B model reaches 86.9% pair accuracy with reasoning and 48.0% without. A post-reasoning weight of 75% minimizes the Brier score at 9B and 27B. For selection, the 9B verifier's responses at 80–90% confidence are 92% correct individually but 78% correct after choosing the best of 32 candidates. Policy-aware calibration reduces signed gaps from −11.7 to +20.5 points to −2.7 to +2.1 points across 184 settings. Residual overconfidence reaches 6.1 points on unseen datasets.
sections.heading: Capability and Reliability Analysis
sections.headline: Selecting among candidates makes reported confidence overconfident, and policy-aware calibration narrows the gaps across 184 settings.

sections.body: Both variants run on vLLM, llama.cpp, and MLX, with bidirectional attention implemented separately for each runtime. Top-choice agreement with the reference is 99.5–99.8% on vLLM and 99.4–99.9% for BF16 MLX builds, but the paper notes this does not imply numerical agreement of probabilities. On an H200, BF16 Instant readouts take 24–52 ms at 256 tokens and 31–98 ms at 1,024 tokens, and FP8 reduces latency by approximately 25–30% at 8,192 tokens for the 9B and 27B Instant models. On an Apple M5 Pro with 64 GB, BF16 Instant readouts at 1,024 tokens range from 59 ms at 0.8B to approximately 1.1 s at 9B, and the 27B models need quantization to run locally. `Q4_K_M` can incur a 4.3-point loss on DecisionPivot for the 27B AutoThink model, while FP8 and `Q8_0` largely preserve decision performance.
sections.heading: Efficient Inference and Deployment
sections.headline: Single-pass Instant readouts on a single GPU take 24–52 ms for 256-token prompts and 31–98 ms for 1,024-token prompts.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes StartLux-Decision as a set of models with a single-pass Instant variant and a reasoning-enabled AutoThink variant that share a probability interface. It credits RLCD2 with better reasoning termination and efficiency while largely preserving held-out accuracy. It cites strong results on Decision Index and DecisionPivot, and policy-aware calibration for selection and routing effects. It notes runtime support across vLLM, llama.cpp, and MLX for GPU and local inference. The stated limits are generalization beyond represented task families and reliability under distribution shift, which the authors name as future work. The section reports no new measurements.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Future work targets generalization beyond represented task families and reliability under distribution shift.

sections.body: Appendix A describes the record format, parent-group splitting, Lux-Release with about 2.7 million records for 0.8B–9B and 0.8 million for 27B, and Lux-Rounds with about 1.7 million records. It states that training records are screened against Decision Index, public JevBench items, and DecisionPivot. Appendix B covers bidirectional attention, which produces outputs bit-identical to the causal implementation when disabled, and direct probability optimization, which reduces calibration error from 5.1 to 3.9 points at 4B. Appendix C gives propositions on selection-induced overconfidence and routing, and shows that marginal certification does not imply route-wise certification. Appendix D covers long option lists, with 86.7% accuracy on 151-option intent questions versus 95.7% for 26 options, and requires at least 99.9% request completion for valid evaluation runs.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix documents training data sources and decontamination, policy-aware calibration proofs, and serving configuration safeguards.
